analysis.one_liner: Bars colleges receiving federal student aid from misleading ads about licensed-career programs.
analysis.headline: A bill to stop colleges from misleading students about licensing requirements never got a committee vote or hearing in the 112th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Senator Jeff Merkley introduced the Protecting Students from Worthless Degrees Act on August 1, 2012. It targeted a specific problem: colleges marketing programs for occupations that require a state license, when the program does not actually qualify a graduate to get that license. The bill would have made it illegal for colleges receiving federal student aid to advertise that students can work in a licensed occupation when that is not true. It also would have required colleges to tell out-of-state and online applicants whether their program meets the licensing rules in the student's own state. The bill was read twice and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced. It never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote, and the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 without the bill moving any further.
analysis.who_benefits: Prospective students considering programs aimed at licensed occupations — nursing, dental hygiene, and similar fields — especially those enrolling online or from out of state, who currently have no federal guarantee that a college must tell them whether its program meets their state's licensing requirements. Students borrowing federal loans (Title IV aid) to pay for programs that don't lead to licensure would be spared that debt, and taxpayers who back those loans would save money.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students and taxpayers backing their loans

how_it_helps.text: Colleges receiving federal student aid (Title IV of the Higher Education Act) would be barred from advertising or telling prospective students that they can work in a recognized occupation that requires a license or other entry requirements, when that is not the case.
The bill would require a college to notify out-of-state applicants whether its program satisfies the licensing or entry requirements of the state where the student lives or intends to enroll.

Because most career-college students pay with federal loans and grants backed by taxpayers, cutting off misleading marketing for programs that do not lead to licensure would reduce wasted borrowing and taxpayer exposure.

analysis.who_pays: Institutions of higher education that participate in federal student aid programs and would have faced new limits on how they advertise licensed-career programs — chiefly career colleges and any school whose marketing implies licensure readiness the program does not deliver. All covered institutions would bear new compliance costs for disclosures and recordkeeping, and schools could face legal liability under the bill's provisions.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have imposed compliance obligations on every institution of higher education that participates in Title IV federal student aid, including honest public and nonprofit colleges, with disclosure and recordkeeping costs and possible legal liability for marketing statements.

Critics would note that state licensing boards already publish their entry requirements, so a student who researches a program's accreditation and licensure pass rates can learn much of this without a federal mandate; the bill targets one gap (out-of-state notification) in a broader problem.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete but targeted: students at career-oriented programs would get an honest answer about whether a degree leads to a license, and taxpayers would stop backing loans for programs that cannot deliver one. The costs fall mostly on institutions that profit from such marketing, plus some compliance burden on well-behaved colleges. On balance the protection is real and the cost is modest, though the bill addresses marketing claims rather than program quality itself.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and immediately referred to the Senate HELP Committee, which never took it up before the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Merkley introduced S. 3474 on August 1, 2012; the Senate read it twice and referred it the same day to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
That was the only action ever taken: the committee held no hearing, reported no vote, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2013 with the bill still parked there.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Institutions that rely on federal student aid revenue and would have been constrained by the new marketing rules — particularly career colleges whose recruiting depends on claims about licensed careers — are better off, since the status quo they operate under never changed. Students who might have been spared misleading marketing gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar Title IV institutions from misleading advertising about licensed-career programs and require out-of-state licensure disclosures.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.role: Committee that controlled the bill's fate
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or vote on the bill after it was referred on the day of introduction.

against.name: For-profit college industry
against.role: Career-college sector whose recruiters depend on federal student aid
against.what_they_did: This sector's lobbying operations were heavily active in Washington during this period against consumer-protection rules aimed at career-college recruiting; the record here does not show a direct campaign on this specific bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll call to divide; all sponsorship was Democratic — Merkley plus three Democratic cosponsors — with no Republican support on record.

industries.note: These schools draw most of their revenue from federal Title IV student aid, and the bill would have restricted marketing claims about programs for licensed occupations — a core recruiting tool where programs do not lead to licensure. The bill never advanced, so the status quo was preserved.

The bill covered all Title IV institutions, adding disclosure and compliance costs, but honest public and nonprofit colleges that accurately describe licensure outcomes would face little practical change.
Taxpayers back student loans for programs whose marketing overstates licensure outcomes; blocking those claims would reduce defaulted federal lending.
